title: Volumes of revolution
examples: When do I use discs instead of washers?
What is the difference between revolving around the x-axis versus the y-axis?
How do I set up the integral if the function is given in terms of y?

explain.say: Today we learn about volumes of revolution. We find the volume when a shape spins around an axis. This uses integration methods.

draw.text: Volumes of Revolution: Discs and Washers

explain.say: First we look at the disc method. This is used when the cross-section is solid, with no hole in the middle. Think of spinning a simple curve.
The volume formula for discs is pi times radius squared times the thickness. If rotating around the x-axis, the thickness is dx.
Next we use the washer method. This is for shapes with a hole in the center. We find the area of the big circle minus the small circle.
For cross-sections, we find the area of the slice perpendicular to the axis. The volume is then the integral of these cross-sectional areas.

items: Volume is integral of these areas

faq.q: When should I use the disc method versus the washer method?
faq.a: Use the disc method when the region being rotated touches the axis of rotation. Use the washer method when there is a gap between the region and the axis.
asks: Do I always need a hole for washers?
When is the disc method simpler?

faq.q: What does the radius represent in these formulas?
faq.a: The radius is the distance from the axis of rotation to the boundary of the shape. You must measure this distance correctly.
asks: How do I find the radius?
Is the radius always the function value?

faq.q: If I rotate around the y-axis, what changes in my integral?
faq.a: You must use the variable y for your integration and express your functions in terms of y. The thickness becomes dy.
asks: Does the axis change the variable?
What if I use dy instead of dx?

faq.q: What is the thickness when I integrate with respect to x?
faq.a: When integrating with respect to x, the thickness is always dx. This means we are summing up infinitesimally thin slices along the x-axis.
asks: Does dx mean I use x in the integral?

faq.q: How do I handle cross-sections if the axis is slanted?
faq.a: For slanted axes, the problem usually requires a coordinate rotation or a more advanced setup. For standard problems, the axis is usually horizontal or vertical.
asks: Can I use this method for slanted axes?
What if the cross-section isn't perpendicular?

facts: The disc method applies when the cross-section is solid.
The washer method is used when the cross-section has a hole.
If rotating around the x-axis, the thickness element is dx.
The volume is found by integrating the cross-sectional area over an interval.

quiz.say: A region under y = x^2 from x equals zero to x equals two is revolved around the x-axis. What is the volume?
quiz.why: This is a disc method problem revolving around the x-axis, so the radius is x squared.

wrong.1: This mistake might come from forgetting to square the radius function.
wrong.2: This mistake might come from integrating x^2 instead of x^4.
wrong.3: This mistake might come from using the wrong limits of integration.

quiz.say: A cross-section perpendicular to the y-axis has an area given by A(y) = y. What is the volume from y equals zero to y equals four?
quiz.why: Since the area is given as a function of y, the thickness must be dy, making this a direct integration.

wrong.0: This mistake might result from calculating the area at the endpoint instead of integrating.
wrong.1: This mistake forgets to multiply the result by the thickness element.
wrong.2: This mistake might come from calculating the area at the endpoint only.
